title: Angle Bisector — Verifying with the tan θ Method
topicTitle: Pair of straight lines: general equation of second degree in x and y, condition for representing a pair of lines, homogenous second-degree equation in x and y, angle between pair of lines, bisectors of the angles between pair of lines
notes: As a cross-check, find the angle θ between one of the original lines and one candidate bisector using: tan θ = |(m₁ − m_b)/(1 + m₁·m_b)|, where m₁ is the original line's slope and m_b is the bisector's slope
**If tan θ < 1** (θ < 45°): since θ is half the angle between the two original lines, the total angle is less than 90°, so this bisector is the **acute** angle bisector
**If tan θ > 1** (θ > 45°): this bisector is the **obtuse** angle bisector
**Worked check:** slope of Bisector 1 (6x + 6y − 1 = 0) is m_b = −6/6 = −1; with the original line's slope m₁ = −1/2: tan θ = |(−1/2 − (−1))/(1 + (−1/2)(−1))| = |(1/2)/(3/2)| = 1/3
Since tan θ = 1/3 < 1, this confirms 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 is definitively the **acute angle bisector** — matching the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method

mindmap.centralConcept: Pair of straight lines from a second-degree equation

subtopics.name: General second-degree equation
points: Represents a pair of straight lines when a specific condition holds
The condition is abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0

subtopics.name: Homogeneous equation
points: ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 always represents two lines through the origin
Divide by x^2 to get a quadratic in (y/x)
The two roots are the slopes of the two lines

subtopics.name: Angle between the lines
points: Lines are perpendicular when a + b = 0
Lines are coincident when h^2 = ab

subtopics.name: Bisectors and combined properties
points: The bisectors of a homogeneous pair are given by h(x^2 - y^2) = (a - b)xy
Sum and product of slopes come from the quadratic in y/x
The non-homogeneous case factorises into two lines not necessarily through the origin

subtopics.name: Exam technique
points: Check the condition for a pair of lines before factorising
Factorise by treating the equation as a quadratic in one variable
Verify by expanding the factorised form back
